ety.text: From Middle English saien, sain, san, secgan, segen, seien, sein, seiȝen, sugen, sægen, ziggen, from Old English seċġan, secgean, secggan, secggean, seggan, sæċġan (“to say, speak”), from Proto-West Germanic *saggjan, from Proto-Germanic *sagjaną (“to say”), from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷ-h₁-yé-, a suffixed o-grade form of *sekʷ- (“to say”).
From Middle French saie, from Latin saga, plural of sagum (“military cloak”).

ex: Please say your name slowly and clearly.
Martha, will you say the Pledge of Allegiance?

senses.d: To tell, either verbally or in writing.
ex: He said he would be here tomorrow.
The note I think he said she wrote is nowhere to be found.

senses.d: To indicate in a written form.
ex: The sign says it’s 50 kilometres to Paris.
What time does it say on the clock?

senses.d: To have a common expression; used in singular passive voice or plural active voice to indicate a rumor or well-known fact.
ex: They say "when in Rome, do as the Romans do", which means "behave as those around you do."
They say that Hope is happiness; But genuine Love must prize the past.

senses.d: Suppose, assume; used to mark an example, supposition or hypothesis.
ex: A holiday somewhere warm – Florida, say – would be nice.
Say he refuses. What do we do then?

senses.d: To speak; to express an opinion; to make answer; to reply.
ex: You have said; but whether wisely or no, let the forest judge
To this argument we shall soon have said; for what concerns it us to hear a husband divulge his household privacies?

senses.d: To bet as a wager on an outcome; by extension, used to express belief in an outcome by the speaker.
ex: 'My fifty pounds says three months after the invasion there'll be a free press in Iraq, and unmonitored internet access too.'

senses.d: A chance to speak; the right or power to influence or make a decision.
ex: The local government did not have much say in the matter.
Above all, however, we would like to think that there is more to be decided, after the engines and after the humans have had their says.
Pick a color you think they'd like, say, peach.
He was driving pretty fast, say, fifty miles per hour.

senses.d: Used to gain someone's attention before making an inquiry or suggestion
ex: Say, what did you think about the movie?

senses.d: A type of fine cloth similar to serge.
ex: All in a kirtle of diſcolourd ſay / He clothed was […]
I, that had sayed on one of his customers sutes.
If those principal works of God […] be but certain tastes and says, as if were, of that final benefit.
Thy tongue some say of breeding breathes.
He found a sword of better say.
This fellow, Captaine, Will come, in time, to be a great distiller, And giue a say[…]at the philosophers stone.

Proto-Indo-European *tḱey- Proto-Indo-European *-né- Proto-Indo-European *-ti Proto-Indo-European *tḱinéti Proto-Italic *sinō Proto-Italic *pozinō Latin pono Spanish poner Inherited from Latin pōnere (whence English post and position), from Proto-Italic *pozinō.

ex:

ety.text: Renaissance borrowing of Latin dictum, with francisation of the ending. Doublet of dit.

ety.text: Inherited from Latin dictus. In some Old Spanish texts, it originally appeared as decho; it was later altered with the influence of the -i- from conjugated forms of decir (e.g. digo, dice, diga, etc.), or a result of metaphony from palatalization. Compare English dictum.
Borrowed from French refrain. Compare Catalan refrany.
From the past participle of ditar; cf. also Latin dictātum, dictātus.
